description: Fast, full fists are a readout of the most underrated strength in your hands: tendon travel. Retake the fist test as a strength test, learn why glide decides grip endurance for hangs and climbs, and get the routine that turns sticky cables into silk ones.

scenes.narration: Hand up, fingers spread wide and straight. Now close the tightest fist you own, fingertips into the palm, and open again completely. That full swing is one rep, and for thirty seconds you will count how many complete swings your hand can make, no half fists, no fingers that skip the last centimeter of straight. You have taken this test as a stiffness check. Take it today as a strength test, because the thing it measures, how far and how freely your finger tendons travel, is the hidden machinery under grip endurance: how long you can hang, climb, and hold before your hands quit. Muscles pull the cables. The cables' travel decides what the pulling is worth. Count both hands. Keep both numbers. At the end, I will show you the machinery.

beats.text: THE SLOW HAND IS THE STORY

scenes.label: FULL FISTS IN THIRTY SECONDS
scenes.narration: Twenty full fists is free travel. Twenty six or more is silk. Under twelve is a hand whose cables drag through their tunnels, spending effort on friction that should have gone into grip. Read this as an athlete for once. When you hang from a bar, your fingers must stay fully closed around it for minutes, and every millimeter of tendon travel must happen against load, through the same tunnels this test just audited. A hand with sticky glide fatigues like a brake left half on: the forearm burns early, the fingers open against your will, and the set ends with your muscles still willing. The fist count is the cheapest possible audit of that system, and the slower hand is always the story, because hangs fail at the weaker hand's travel, not the stronger one's.
scenes.sub: under 12: the cables drag - over 26: silk cables

scenes.narration: Look at the budget your fingers spend. The tendons that close your hand run from your forearm through tunnels in the wrist and palm, out to the fingertips, and a single full fist requires them to glide centimeters through those tunnels. Now multiply: a dead hang is one long held fist, a climbing session is hundreds of loaded ones, and every single rep pays a friction tax set by the quality of the glide. When the tunnels are supple and the cables slide, the tax is tiny and your forearm's strength reaches your fingers almost intact. When the glide is sticky, the tax compounds with every rep until the hand opens early, not from weak muscles but from expensive ones. This is the hidden strength the title means. Nobody's forearm grew during a month of glide work. But the strength they already owned started arriving at the fingertips at full value, and their hangs doubled like a magic trick with a mechanical explanation.

The morning melt is your progress meter, and it deserves a second look. Stiff fingers at dawn that loosen within minutes of moving are reporting friction: tunnels that sat still all night in stale fluid, cables that need their first travels to redistribute it. That pattern is the friendliest diagnosis in this entire season, because friction responds to exactly one thing, repeated gentle travel, and it responds measurably: the melt gets faster week by week, and the fist count climbs with it. Track both numbers together and you have a dashboard no app sells. The count tells you the travel. The melt tells you the friction. When both improve, your grip endurance is improving in the background of your life, and one day a hang that used to end at forty seconds ends at ninety and you will know exactly which invisible system to thank.

lines: a different part of the travel.
beats.title: THE FULL MAP

scenes.narration: The glide sequence earns its place in a strength episode, and here is why. Straight hand, hook fist, full fist: each position slides the two finger tendons by different amounts against each other and against their tunnels, so the full sequence audits the entire travel map instead of just the comfortable middle of it. Sticky spots hide at the extremes, the last degrees of opening and the final squeeze of closing, which are precisely the positions gripping sports live in. A hand trained only in the middle of its map feels strong in the middle of its map. The sequence is how you pave the whole road. Do it slowly, with a pause at each position, and you are not doing rehab homework anymore. You are doing the finger equivalent of a full-range strength program, at the exact joints where your grip will be won and lost.

lines: A hundred full travels a day
beats.title: THE INVISIBLE PROGRAM

scenes.narration: Here is the skinny advantage in your hands, and it is almost unfair. Glide work costs zero recovery, needs zero equipment, and can be hidden inside any day: at a desk, in a queue, mid-conversation, a hundred full travels before lunch. Thicker, heavier hands fight more tissue drag per rep and swell more for their efforts. Yours can run an invisible training program at a volume no other tissue in this season tolerates, and glide is a tissue quality that pays out in direct proportion to total travels banked. A month of invisible reps later, your hands close faster, fuller, and cheaper than the hands of men with forearms twice your size, and their hangs end first. There is no photograph of this advantage. There is only the bar, and who is still on it.

Train with me. Full open to full fist, as fast as the full range honestly allows, thirty seconds on, fifteen off, four rounds. Both hands. If the range shrinks, slow down: range first, speed second, always.

beats.text: GLIDES BEFORE BED AND AT DAWN
FIST SETS THREE DAYS A WEEK

scenes.narration: Here is your edge plan. The glide sequence twice a day at minimum, dawn and before bed, because the night is when the tunnels set and the morning is when they are audited. Full fist sets three days a week for the speed chapter. Grip training continues as normal, and it will quietly feel different as the friction tax falls. The mistakes to retire: squeeze ball only, forever, retired, closing is one third of the map. Forcing the last degrees of a stuck finger, retired, cables hate violence. Testing your fist count every morning and sulking at the weather, retired, test monthly and train daily. And the standing rule: a finger that locks or snaps painfully, one joint that stays swollen, or stiffness that never melts at all means see a professional if it persists. Those are specific mechanical stories, and they have specific fixes that videos cannot deliver.

beats.text: UNDER 12 = A TAX ON EVERY GRIP

scenes.narration: So, your count. Under twelve: every grip you own is paying a friction tax, and the glide routine is about to hand you strength you technically already had. Twelve to twenty: the tax is falling, keep the travels coming and watch the melt shorten. Over twenty: your cables run clean, and your hands will outlast forearms much bigger than yours. Comment your count and your morning melt time, because together they are the dashboard. In thirty days we count fists again, first thing, honest rules. Your hidden strength was never only in the muscle. It was in the travel, and travel can be trained.

Your hands were built to hold on. Give their cables a clean road and they will. Glide a little every day, and in thirty days we count together. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Fist Test Reveals Your Hidden Strength
